title: The Queer Nonverbal Dialect
hook: “Gaydar” feels like reading; the research says it mostly measures stereotypes, and acting on it can out someone who never chose to be seen.
why:
Most men have, at some point, looked at another man and wondered whether he was gay. Popular culture calls the supposed ability to tell gaydar, and many people believe they have it. This chapter is partly about whether that belief holds up, and mostly about what to do instead of acting on it.

Gay, bisexual and other queer men do have their own nonverbal dialect: ways of signalling to each other, of testing whether it is safe to be open, of showing interest or affection under conditions where being misread can be dangerous. That dialect deserves understanding and respect. But it is not a code for outsiders to crack. The more useful skill, for most readers, is knowing when not to read at all.

This chapter covers what the research on gaydar actually found, why lab accuracy collapses in the real world, what guessing costs the people guessed about, how the dialect works and why it is so often deliberately ambiguous, attraction between men, which the chapter on attraction in Part III promised to return to, and how to be a reader in whose company people feel safe.

teach.h: Why this chapter is mostly about not reading.
teach.p:
Every other chapter in this book teaches you to notice more. This one asks you to notice something and then put it down. Sexual orientation is not a behaviour, a mood or an intention. It is part of who someone is, and whether to share it, with whom and when, is entirely their decision.

The temptation to read it anyway is strong, and it usually comes from curiosity rather than malice. But a reading of orientation is not like a reading of tiredness or tension. If you are wrong, you have attached a label to someone that may follow them. If you are right and you act on it, by asking, hinting, telling others or treating them differently, you have taken a decision that was theirs to make.

In many workplaces and families this decision still carries real risk. In some countries same-sex relationships remain illegal. Even in more accepting places, many people choose carefully whom to tell, and when. Being guessed about removes that choice.

So the discipline of this chapter is restraint. Notice that you are wondering, recognise that it is not your question to answer, and return to reading the person in front of you as an individual: their mood, their comfort, their wish to talk or be left alone. The figure here stands at rest. Nothing about how he stands tells you whom he loves, and nothing needs to.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if guessing at someone's orientation carried no risk for them. People who are outed without their consent describe loss of control over a deeply personal decision, and in some places guessing can expose people to danger.

teach.p:
Psychologists have tested gaydar directly. In 2008 Nicholas Rule and Nalini Ambady showed observers photographs of men's faces, taken from dating profiles, for as little as a twentieth of a second, and asked them to judge whether each man was gay or straight. Observers did better than chance, but not by much: in the briefest condition, they were right roughly 57 per cent of the time, where guessing would give 50.

In 2007 Kerri Johnson and her colleagues studied body movement. Observers watched animated figures and filmed people walking, and judged their orientation. They relied heavily on gender stereotypes: men who walked with a sway of the hips, rather than a swagger of the shoulders, were judged gay. With real walkers, observers were right somewhat more than 60 per cent of the time for men, and no better than chance for women.

These findings are often reported as proof that gaydar is real. A more careful reading is that, in a laboratory, with a set of photographs or walkers in which half are gay, people do slightly better than a coin toss, mostly by using stereotypes about gender.

That is a modest result, and the next block shows why it shrinks almost to nothing outside the lab. The figure here walks with an ordinary stride. Observers in these studies would have been confident about him, one way or the other, and often wrong.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if observers judged orientation from faces or walks with high accuracy. In these studies, accuracy was only modestly above chance, and largely driven by gender stereotypes.

teach.h: Why lab accuracy fails on the street.
teach.p:
In most laboratory studies, about half the people shown are gay. In real life the proportion is far smaller: surveys in many countries put the share of people who identify as gay or lesbian at a few per cent. This matters enormously.

Suppose you could tell gay from straight men with 60 per cent accuracy, better than most studies found. In a room of a hundred men where five are gay, you would correctly pick out three of the five. But you would also wrongly label about thirty-eight of the ninety-five straight men as gay. Most of your gay guesses would be wrong. Researchers call this the false positive paradox.

In 2016 William Cox, Janet Hyde and their colleagues went further. They found that the apparent accuracy of judgments from faces could be explained by differences in the photographs, such as image quality, rather than anything about the faces. They also found that people readily inferred orientation from stereotypes about fashion, interests and jobs. And when participants were told that gaydar was real, they stereotyped more.

The researchers concluded that gaydar works less as a skill than as a licence to stereotype. Believing in it makes people more willing to apply assumptions about how gay men look and behave, and those assumptions are wrong about most people. The figure here sits with his chin on his hand, thinking. Thinking carefully about this question leads to the conclusion that it cannot be answered by looking.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if real-world guesses about orientation were mostly correct. Because gay people are a small minority, even modest lab accuracy produces mostly wrong guesses in everyday life.
teach.pullQuote: Gaydar works less as a skill than as a licence to stereotype.

teach.p:
Speculating about whether a colleague, a friend or a relative is gay can feel harmless, even affectionate. It rarely is.

Being the subject of speculation is uncomfortable for anyone. For someone who is gay and has not told people, it creates a choice they did not want: deny it, confirm it on someone else's timetable, or live with the gossip. For someone who is straight, it attaches a label based on how they walk, speak or dress, which often means it attaches to men who do not fit narrow ideas of masculinity. Boys and men who are gentle, artistic or uninterested in sport have long been targeted with exactly these guesses.

Speculation also tells the people around you something about you. A gay colleague who hears others guessing about someone else learns that this is a place where people are watched and discussed. That is information they will use when deciding whether to be open.

The practical rule is simple. Do not speculate aloud, do not join in when others do, and do not ask someone directly whether they are gay unless you have a real reason and a relationship that can bear it. If someone wants you to know, they will tell you. The figures here stand in a small group, the kind of circle in which a careless guess about someone outside it travels fast.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if speculation about orientation had no effect on the people speculated about or those who overheard it. Gay men's accounts of choosing whether to come out at work and in families consistently describe weighing how others talk about people like them.

teach.p:
Queer men do have nonverbal ways of recognising and signalling to one another, and they are worth understanding, not so that outsiders can decode them, but so that they can understand why they work as they do.

Because being openly gay has often been dangerous, many of these signals are deliberately ambiguous. A glance held a beat longer than usual. A reference to a partner without a gender. A mention of a bar, a film or a neighbourhood that means something to those who know. Each of these can be read by someone who shares the dialect and passed over by someone who does not, which is the point. They allow people to find each other while keeping deniability if the reading turns out to be wrong, or the person turns out to be hostile.

This is a familiar pattern in any group that has needed to be careful: signals designed to be read by insiders and missed by everyone else. The next chapter looks at how the same need for safety shapes what couples do in public.

For a reader who is not part of the dialect, two lessons follow. First, ambiguity is often deliberate, and resolving it by asking or guessing defeats its purpose. Second, if someone does use a gender-neutral word for their partner, follow their lead and use it too until they choose otherwise. The figure here tilts his head, listening. Some things said to him will carry a second layer of meaning, intended for someone else.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if the signals queer men use to find each other were mostly unambiguous. Their deliberate ambiguity, allowing deniability, reflects the risks that openness has carried.

teach.p:
The chapter on attraction in Part III dealt mainly with men reading women, and promised to return to attraction between men. The core of that chapter applies unchanged. Interest shows mainly as attention: turning toward someone, staying close, asking questions, touching briefly, holding a gaze. Men tend to overread interest. Friendliness is not desire. The only reliable reading is a clear answer to a question, and no means no.

Between men, there is an added layer of uncertainty. Neither person may know whether the other is gay or bisexual, and getting it wrong can be embarrassing or, with a hostile person, dangerous. So signals of interest are often subtler and more deniable, and they are tested gradually, as the previous block described.

Two kinds of misreading follow. A gay or bisexual man may read friendliness from a straight man as interest. A straight man may read ordinary warmth from a gay man as a pass, and react with discomfort or hostility. The chapters on the bro hug and on space between men in Part III described how the fear of seeming gay has shaped how straight men touch and stand. That fear, which researchers have called homohysteria, has eased in many places but not disappeared.

The response is the same as with anyone. If you are interested, ask, with room for no. If you are not, say so kindly and clearly, as you would to a woman, without contempt. The figures here stand at an angle, close enough to talk and far enough that either can step away: the right distance for a question.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if attraction between men followed entirely different rules from attraction in general. The same signals and the same hard limits apply; the added uncertainty about orientation and safety mainly makes signals subtler.

teach.p:
For most readers of this book, the most useful thing to learn about queer body language is how their own body language is read by queer people.

When a same-sex couple holds hands in the street or kisses goodbye at a station, respond exactly as you would to any couple, which usually means not responding at all. A stare, a double take or a nudge to a friend is noticed, and remembered. When a colleague mentions a husband or a boyfriend, ask about their weekend in the same tone you would use with anyone. Surprise, even friendly surprise, tells them they were not what you expected.

Use neutral words, such as partner, until you are told otherwise. Do not assume that the man in front of you is straight, or that his wife is the person he lives with. When others make jokes or guesses about someone's orientation, a quiet change of subject, or a plain Leave it, does more than you might think.

None of this requires you to understand the queer dialect. It requires you to make your own body language easy to read: relaxed, unsurprised, interested in the person rather than the category. The figures here are two men walking hand in hand. The most helpful thing a passer-by can do is nothing at all.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if the reactions of passers-by and colleagues made no difference to whether gay people felt safe being open. Gay men consistently describe reading the room for exactly these reactions before deciding how open to be.

caseStudy:
Matt, twenty-nine, works in a sales team of eight men. A new colleague, Dan, joined in the spring: friendly, well dressed, uninterested in football. Within a fortnight, two of the others had decided he was gay, and the guessing had become a running joke when Dan was out of the room. Matt laughed along, though it made him slightly uncomfortable.

One afternoon Dan came back to his desk earlier than expected and caught the end of a joke. Nobody said anything. Dan went quiet for the rest of the day and ate lunch alone for the next week.

Matt thought about it that evening. He realised he had no idea whether Dan was gay, that it was none of his business, and that the joke had told Dan something about the team whichever way it went. The next time it started, he said, quietly, Leave it, he's a good bloke. The others shrugged, and it stopped.

A few months later, at a team dinner, Dan mentioned his husband in passing, testing the water. Matt asked what his husband did for a living and how long they had been together, exactly as he would have with anyone. Dan relaxed visibly. Later he told Matt he had been close to leaving the job in the spring, and that the change in the office had been the reason he stayed. Matt had not thought of two words, Leave it, as a decision that might keep someone in a job. He thought about it often afterwards.
observe: Notice any moment this week when you wonder about someone's orientation, and practise putting the question down.
Notice how people around you react to same-sex couples in public, and what those reactions would tell a gay man watching.
Notice the words you use for people's partners, and whether you assume a gender before you are told.
Notice jokes or guesses about someone's orientation, and how the people present respond.

drills.name: Put the Question Down
steps: The next time you find yourself wondering whether someone is gay, notice it.
Ask yourself what you would do with the answer if you had it.
Recognise that the question is theirs to answer, not yours.
Return your attention to something you can actually read: their mood, comfort or wish to talk.
variations: When you notice the question in your mind, write down the stereotype it rests on, and check whether you would apply it to anyone else.
Notice whether the question arises more often about men who are gentle, artistic or uninterested in sport, and what that tells you.
Put the question down for a whole month, and notice whether anything about your relationship with the person changes.

drills.name: Neutral by Default
steps: For one week, use partner rather than wife or girlfriend when asking about someone's life, until they tell you more.
Notice how often you would otherwise have assumed.
When someone tells you about their partner, mirror the words they use.
Note any moment where the neutral word made a conversation easier.
variations: Change one form, invitation or template at work so that it says partner rather than wife or husband.
Ask a friend how they would like their partner referred to when you introduce them, and use their answer.
Notice how many times in a week someone assumes your own partner's gender, or would if you had one.

drills.name: The Quiet Interruption
steps: Prepare one short line you could use to end speculation about someone's orientation, such as Leave it, it's his business.
Practise saying it in a calm, ordinary tone.
The next time speculation starts, use it.
Afterwards, note how the group responded.
variations: Practise a version of the interruption for a family gathering as well as for work, since jokes often feel harder to stop at home.
Agree with a friend that you will back each other up if either of you interrupts a joke.
Notice how long it takes for a group to move on after a quiet interruption, which is usually only a few seconds.

drills.name: Unremarkable
steps: The next time you see a same-sex couple showing affection in public, notice your first reaction.
Practise letting your face and body stay exactly as they would for any couple.
Reflect on what a stare or a double take would have communicated.
Write one sentence about what you noticed in yourself.
variations: Notice your reaction to an on-screen same-sex couple, and practise the same stillness you would show any couple.
Notice whether anyone around you reacts to a same-sex couple in public, and whether you could, safely, simply carry on as normal beside them.
Ask yourself what a same-sex couple would need to see from strangers to feel safe holding hands on your street.

quiz.q: A friend says he can always tell who is gay just by looking. What does the research suggest?
options: He is right, since lab studies show people judge orientation from faces with very high accuracy
Lab accuracy is only slightly above chance, and in real life most such guesses would be wrong
Nobody can ever do better than chance, so the studies all found exactly fifty per cent accuracy
Only gay men can tell, because they share the same signals and nobody else can read them
quiz.explain: Observers in lab studies do only modestly better than chance. Because gay people are a small minority, even that accuracy produces mostly wrong guesses in everyday life.

quiz.q: In Rule and Ambady's 2008 study, how accurate were observers who saw men's faces for a twentieth of a second?
options: About 57 per cent, where guessing would give 50
About 95 per cent, close to perfect accuracy
Exactly 50 per cent, no better than guessing
About 30 per cent, worse than random guessing
quiz.explain: Observers did slightly better than chance in the laboratory. Later work questioned whether even that came from the faces or from differences in the photographs.

quiz.q: What did Johnson and colleagues find observers relied on when judging orientation from how people walked?
options: The length of each stride, which observers measured very precisely
The speed of walking, with faster walkers judged straight every time
Gender stereotypes, judging hip sway in men as a sign of being gay
Nothing in particular, since observers guessed entirely at random
quiz.explain: Observers linked gender-atypical movement, such as hip sway in men, to being gay. Accuracy with real walkers was modestly above chance for men and at chance for women.

quiz.q: What did Cox and colleagues find when they told participants that gaydar was real?
options: Participants became more accurate at judging orientation from faces alone
Participants refused to make any judgments about orientation at all
Participants judged everyone to be straight, whatever they were shown
Participants relied more on stereotypes when judging orientation
quiz.explain: Believing in gaydar made people more willing to apply stereotypes. The researchers concluded that gaydar works more as a licence to stereotype than as a skill.

quiz.q: A colleague mentions in passing that he and his husband went walking at the weekend. What fits this chapter best?
options: Ask where they walked and how long they have been together, as you would anyone
Say you had no idea he was gay, so that he knows you are fine with it
Change the subject quickly, so that neither of you feels uncomfortable
Tell the rest of the team afterwards, so they know not to make jokes
quiz.explain: Responding in the same tone you would use with anyone tells him that this is unremarkable. Surprise, even friendly surprise, signals that he was not what you expected.

quiz.q: At a bar, a man you do not know holds your gaze and comes over to talk. You are not interested. What fits this chapter best?
options: Make it clear you find the idea offensive, so he does not try again
Be friendly and say plainly that you are not interested, as with anyone
Ignore him completely and turn your back until he goes away again
Play along to avoid awkwardness, then leave when he goes to the bar
quiz.explain: The same principles apply as with any approach: a clear, kind answer, without contempt. Hostility to a gay man's interest is a reaction to the category, not to anything he did.

quiz.q: Why do laboratory findings of above-chance gaydar fail to work in everyday life?
options: Because laboratory photographs are always of famous people, whom observers already know
Because far fewer people are gay than in the lab sets, so most guesses would be wrong
Because people in real life always tell you their orientation within the first minute
Because gaydar only works for women, while most real-life guesses are about men
quiz.explain: Lab sets are often about half gay, while in real life the share is small. Even modest accuracy then produces mostly false positives, which is the false positive paradox.

quiz.q: A teacher hears a boy say "That's so gay" to a classmate in the changing room. What fits this chapter best?
options: Ask the classmate in front of the others whether he is gay, so that the matter is cleared up
Interrupt quietly and plainly, keep the target out of it, and address the word with the class later
Ignore it, since it is just banter and the boys will grow out of it on their own in time
Lecture the boy loudly in front of the whole room, so that everyone can see him being punished for it
quiz.explain: A quiet, plain interruption changes what the room thinks is acceptable without making the target the topic. Guessing about the boy's orientation would add to the harm.

quiz.q: Someone says that a bisexual man dating a woman is really straight, and one dating a man is really gay. What does this chapter suggest?
options: That orientation is what a person tells you, not what you infer from their partner
That a partner's gender is always the most reliable sign of a person's real orientation
That bisexual men are usually confused, and will settle on one orientation in time
That orientation can be read accurately from how a couple behaves together in public
quiz.explain: Bisexual people are often reread according to their partner, which ignores what they have said about themselves. When someone tells you their orientation, believe them.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific time you wondered about, guessed at or joked about someone's sexual orientation, or heard others do so. Describe what prompted the guess: a way of walking, talking, dressing or not fitting in. What would you have done with the answer? Now imagine you were that person and had overheard. What would it have told you about the people around you? Describe one thing you will do differently the next time the subject comes up.
reflection.guidance: Most men have done this, usually without malice. The point is not guilt but awareness of what guessing costs and communicates. Be specific about the moment and about the alternative: putting the question down, using neutral words, or quietly ending the speculation.

failureMode: The first failure is to believe you can tell someone's orientation by looking, when lab accuracy is barely above chance and real-world guesses are mostly wrong. The second is to speculate aloud or join in when others do, which can out people and tells everyone listening whether it is safe to be open. The third is to ask someone directly when you have no real reason. The fourth is to try to decode the deliberately ambiguous signals queer men use with each other. The fifth is to react to a same-sex couple, or to a colleague's mention of a husband, with visible surprise. And the sixth is to answer a man's interest with contempt rather than a clear, kind no.

moreCases.title: The father who asked at dinner
moreCases.scene:
Ian, fifty-two, has been wondering for a year whether his son, Ollie, sixteen, is gay. Ollie has never had a girlfriend, spends a lot of time with one close friend, Reece, and has lost interest in football, which they used to watch together. Ian has read that parents should be supportive, and he wants Ollie to know that it would be fine.

One evening at dinner, with Ollie's younger sister at the table, Ian puts down his fork and says, warmly, "Ollie, I just want you to know that if you're gay, that's absolutely fine with me and your mum. You can tell us anything." He smiles encouragingly.

Ollie goes bright red. His sister giggles. He says, "I'm not," in a tight voice, eats two more mouthfuls and goes to his room. For the next month he barely speaks to his father, stops inviting Reece round and spends most evenings at Reece's house instead. Ian is baffled and hurt. He had meant it as the kindest thing he could say.

His wife, Sarah, points out, gently, that he had asked a sixteen-year-old the most private question of his life in front of his little sister, over shepherd's pie, on the strength of a guess about football.

He had also, a few weeks earlier, mentioned his suspicion to his own brother over a pint, and his brother had told his wife, who had asked Sarah about it. Ollie, it later turned out, had overheard.

He has also been watching Ollie's phone screen when it lights up on the table, and reading the names of who is messaging him. Ollie has noticed, and has started keeping the phone face down.

Sarah also tells him that she had wondered the same things, and had decided the best thing she could do was make sure Ollie knew the house was safe, and wait.
moreCases.misread:
Ian read Ollie's lack of girlfriends, his close friendship and his drift away from football as signs that he might be gay, and read his own question as support. Ollie read the question as being watched, guessed about and put on the spot in front of his family.

His wife's brother read the same signs the same way, which made the reading feel shared and therefore more likely. Several people guessing is not evidence; it is the same stereotype, repeated.

Ian also read Ollie's "I'm not" as an answer, when it was a boy closing a door that had been opened in front of his sister.

His brother had read Ian's worry as gossip worth passing on, which is how a guess travels round a family.
moreCases.betterRead:
Cox and colleagues found that people readily infer orientation from stereotypes about interests and friendships, and that believing in gaydar makes them more likely to do so. Ian's reading rested on exactly those stereotypes. More importantly, the question was Ollie's to answer, when and to whom he chose. Asking, however warmly, took that choice away and made a guess into a public moment. The better approach, which Ian tried after apologising, was to put the question down and show safety in other ways: reacting warmly to gay characters on television, using neutral words such as partner, stopping his brother-in-law's jokes at a family party. He stopped wondering aloud. Nearly a year later, in the car, Ollie told him that he was bisexual and that Reece was his boyfriend. Ian said, "Thank you for telling me. I like Reece a lot," and kept his eyes on the road.

Ollie told his father later that the moment he decided he could tell him was when Ian told his uncle to stop a joke at Christmas.

Ian also apologised to Ollie's sister, separately, for putting her brother on the spot in front of her.

moreCases.title: The man the club decided about
moreCases.scene:
Rhys, twenty-four, plays rugby for his village club on Saturdays and teaches dance at a primary school during the week. He is straight, has a girlfriend who lives in another city and is softly spoken off the pitch. Within a month of joining the club, several of the players have decided that he is gay. The jokes start in the changing room: about his job, about his clothes, about the girlfriend nobody has met.

Rhys laughs them off at first. Then he stops laughing. He begins changing quickly and leaving before the others have showered. He skips the social evenings. When a teammate makes a remark about him in front of the opposing team, he does not come to training the following week.

One of the older players, Gareth, thirty-eight, has watched it happen. He has a younger brother who is gay and who left this same club fifteen years earlier for the same reason, though nobody at the club knows that. Gareth has never said anything about the jokes. He has laughed at some of them.

After Rhys misses a second week, Gareth rings him. Rhys says he is thinking of joining another club, where nobody knows him.

Rhys's girlfriend, when he tells her on the phone, says that he should just bring her to a match and that would shut them up. Rhys says that is exactly the problem: he should not have to prove anything.

The coach has heard the jokes too. He has assumed that if Rhys minded, he would say so, and that saying something himself would make it a bigger deal than it was.

Gareth also remembers his brother, at seventeen, coming home from training and going straight to his room, and his mother saying that the boy was just tired.
moreCases.misread:
The players read Rhys's job, voice and absent girlfriend as signs that he was gay, and read their jokes as harmless banter. Rhys, being guessed about, read the club as a place where any man who did not fit was a target.

The players also read Rhys's silence at the start as agreement that it was all a laugh, which is how most targets of banter are read until they stop turning up.

Gareth, for years, had read his own laughter as going along with the group rather than as part of what drove men like his brother away.

The coach read his own silence as neutrality, when to Rhys it was one more adult choosing not to see.
moreCases.betterRead:
Johnson and colleagues found that observers judging orientation leaned heavily on gender stereotypes, and this chapter describes how guesses about orientation tend to attach to men who are gentle, artistic or uninterested in narrow ideas of masculinity, whatever their orientation. The cost of the guessing fell on Rhys, who is straight, and would have fallen just as hard on a gay player, who would have learned that the club was not safe. Gareth's better response, late as it was, was the quiet interruption this chapter describes. At the next training session, when a joke started, he said plainly, "Leave it. We nearly lost a good player over this." He also told the captain about his brother. The captain spoke to the squad. Rhys came back. Gareth's brother, when he heard, came to watch a match for the first time in fifteen years.

The club also added a line to its code of conduct about slurs and banter aimed at players' orientation, and the captain read it out at the start of the season.

Rhys stayed at the club for three seasons and was made vice-captain in the last.

moreCases.title: The double take at the station
moreCases.scene:
Chris, forty-five, is waiting for a train on a Monday morning. Beside him on the platform, two men in their thirties, clearly a couple, are saying goodbye; one is catching the train and the other has walked him to the station with their dog. As the train comes in, they kiss briefly, and one of them says, "See you tonight."

Chris does a double take. He does not mean anything by it; it is reflex, the way his head turns. He then glances at the woman next to him, who is also looking, and raises his eyebrows slightly. She half smiles back.

The man getting on the train sees both of them. He sits down two rows ahead of Chris, takes out his phone and does not look up for the rest of the journey. Chris notices that the man's shoulders have gone up, and that when he gets off at the same stop, he walks quickly away.

Chris thinks about it on the way to the office. He considers himself a fair-minded man. He has gay friends. He was not disapproving; he was surprised. But he realises that the man on the train had no way of knowing that, and that the look he had exchanged with the woman on the platform had probably looked, from the outside, like exactly the thing he would have said he was not.

The woman beside him, he realises, had probably read his raised eyebrows as an invitation to share a joke, and had accepted it.

At the office, a colleague mentions her weekend with her girlfriend, and Chris notices that he has to make a small effort to keep his face exactly as it would be for anyone, which tells him something about the morning.

He also remembers, uncomfortably, that his teenage daughter had once told him that his face "does a thing" when gay couples come on television, and that he had laughed it off.
moreCases.misread:
Chris read his own double take as harmless reflex and his glance at the woman as nothing at all. The man getting on the train read both, quite reasonably, as a stranger noticing, commenting and sharing a reaction to his kiss with someone else.

And the woman he glanced at read his glance as permission to share the reaction, so that one stranger's surprise became two.

Chris also read his own fair-mindedness as something the man on the train could see, when all he could see was a face turning and a glance shared.

His colleague's mention of her girlfriend that afternoon was a second test, and he noticed he had nearly failed it in the same small way.
moreCases.betterRead:
A stare, a double take or a nudge to a friend is noticed and remembered, as this chapter describes, and a shared glance between strangers turns a private surprise into a small public judgment. For a same-sex couple, each of these reactions is information about whether it is safe to be affectionate in public, and the next chapter describes how much that calculation shapes queer men's lives. Chris's intention did not change what the man experienced. The better response, which he practised over the following months, was the Unremarkable drill: when he saw a same-sex couple, he let his face and body stay exactly as they would for any couple, which usually meant not reacting at all. He also noticed how often he had done the same double take before, and how rarely he had thought about it.

He also stopped exchanging glances with strangers about anyone, which he found removed a surprising number of small judgments from his day.

He also told the woman on the platform, the next time he saw her, nothing at all, which he decided was the right amount.

moreCases.title: The climber who asked
moreCases.scene:
Sam, twenty-seven, is gay, and he has been going to a climbing gym on Tuesday and Thursday evenings for a year. For the past two months he has often ended up climbing alongside Jordan, twenty-eight, who is friendly, funny and very good on the overhanging routes. Jordan gives him advice, belays for him, stands close when they look at the route map and once put a hand on his shoulder after a hard climb. They have started having a coffee at the café afterwards.

Sam has begun to wonder whether Jordan is interested. He knows that Jordan has never mentioned a girlfriend or a boyfriend. He knows that friendly straight men can be exactly like this. He also knows that getting it wrong could be embarrassing or, with some men, worse.

One Thursday, after coffee, he decides to ask, lightly, as they walk to the car park: "Would you fancy getting a drink sometime? Like a date, I mean. No worries at all if not."

Jordan stops, looks surprised and then smiles. He says, "That's really nice of you to ask. I'm straight, so not a date. But I'd really like to keep climbing with you, and I'm up for a drink as mates." Sam laughs, a little embarrassed, and says that sounds good.

Sam has asked men out before and been told no, mostly kindly. Once, years ago, at a party, a man laughed loudly, told his friends, and Sam left. He has never quite stopped remembering that evening.

He has also, without meaning to, been reading Jordan's body for weeks: every touch, every lingering conversation, every coffee. None of it had told him anything for certain. Only a question could.

Jordan, it turns out, had not thought about it at all. He is friendly with everyone at the gym and had never wondered how it might look.
moreCases.misread:
Sam read Jordan's closeness, advice and touch as possible interest, which is an easy reading to make and often wrong. Jordan had been reading the friendship as exactly that, and had not considered how it might look.

Had Jordan read Sam's question as an insult, as some men do, a kind invitation would have become a humiliation for no reason at all.

Sam, for a moment afterwards, read his own question as a mistake, when it had been exactly the right thing to do.

Jordan, too, could easily have read Sam's question as something to joke about later with friends. He did not, and that choice mattered as much as the answer.
moreCases.betterRead:
The chapter on attraction in Part III described how interest shows as attention and how easily friendliness is overread, and this chapter adds that between men, where neither may know the other's orientation, signals are often subtle and tested gradually. Sam did the right thing: he did not try to decode Jordan's body, which could not have told him, but asked a clear question that left plenty of room to say no. Jordan did the right thing too. He answered the question kindly and plainly, without recoiling, joking or making Sam feel foolish, and offered what he could. This chapter contrasts that kind of clear, warm no with the contempt some men show when another man is interested in them. They climbed together the following Tuesday. A year later, Jordan was at Sam's birthday drinks, and met Sam's boyfriend.

Sam said later that Jordan's answer had made it easier to ask the next man he liked, because it reminded him that a no could be kind.

workedReading.title: Interrupting a slur in the changing room
workedReading.scene:
Martina, thirty-eight, is a PE teacher at a secondary school. After a Year 9 football lesson, she is collecting equipment outside the boys' changing room, where a male colleague is supervising, when she hears several boys laughing and one of them say, "That's so gay, Josh, you even throw like a girl." There is more laughter. Josh, a quiet boy who is better at dance than football, says nothing. Martina's colleague, who is on his phone at the far end of the corridor, does not seem to have heard. She knows that moments like this are where boys learn what is safe to be, and that the other boys in the room, including any who are gay or unsure, are learning it too. She also knows that the worst thing she could do is make Josh the centre of attention, or guess aloud about who he is.

She also remembers her own school, where the same word was used every day and no teacher ever said anything, and a boy in her year who left at fifteen and whom nobody heard from again.

She has also taught Josh for two years and has no idea whether he is gay, straight or anything else, and she reminds herself that this is exactly as it should be.

She has also seen how quickly a word like that spreads through a year group once it goes unchallenged.

steps.label: Hear it as information
steps.text:
She hears two things in the comment: that "gay" is being used as an insult, and that it is being aimed at a boy who does not fit a narrow picture of masculinity. As this chapter describes, guesses and jokes about orientation tend to fall on boys who are gentle or artistic, whatever their orientation. She does not wonder whether Josh is gay. That question is not hers and would not change what she needs to do.

She also notices that the comment combined two insults, one about orientation and one about girls, and that both need addressing.

She also notices her own urge to find out who said it, and decides that the who matters less in this moment than the what.

steps.label: Interrupt quietly
steps.text:
She knocks on the changing-room door, puts her head round it without coming in, and says in a calm, ordinary voice, "Not that word as an insult, please. Get changed, you've got five minutes." She does not shout, lecture or ask who said it. A quiet, plain interruption stops the moment without turning it into a scene, and tells every boy in the room that the word has been noticed.

She also tells her colleague afterwards what she heard, without blame, and asks him to keep an ear out. Supervision is part of how rooms like this become safe.

She keeps her face neutral and her voice level, so that the interruption reads as a rule rather than an outburst. Boys often take a calm adult more seriously than a shouting one.

She also does not wait outside to see what happens next. Lingering would turn a rule into a confrontation.

steps.label: Keep the target out of it
steps.text:
She does not look at Josh, say his name or ask him whether he is all right in front of the others. Doing so would make him the topic of the moment and confirm that he was the one being singled out. Her aim is to change what the room thinks is acceptable, not to draw attention to the boy the comment was about.

She resists the urge to reassure Josh with a look, which, in that moment, the other boys would have seen and read.

She also knows that some boys in the room may be gay or unsure, and that what they see her do will tell them more than anything she says to Josh.

steps.label: Talk to the group later
steps.text:
At the start of the next lesson, with the whole class, she takes two minutes to say that the school does not allow "gay" to be used as an insult, why it matters to people in the room whether or not anyone knows it, and that the same goes for "like a girl". She does not refer to the incident or to any individual. She keeps her voice and her posture steady, and moves on to the lesson.

One boy asks whether it is still all right to say it as a joke among friends. She says no, and explains, briefly, that you never know who in the room it is about.

She also mentions, briefly, that some people in their families, their friends or the class may be gay, and that the word lands on them whether or not anyone knows.

She keeps it short. Two minutes of plain explanation lands better with fourteen-year-olds than twenty minutes of a lecture.

steps.label: Check in without guessing
steps.text:
Later in the week she finds a moment to ask Josh, in passing, how he is finding PE this term, and mentions that the school's dance club is looking for people. She does not ask about the comment or about anything personal. If he wants to tell her something, she has given him an opening; if not, he has had an ordinary, friendly conversation with a teacher who noticed him.

She also lets his form tutor know, without detail, that he was on the receiving end of some name-calling, so that someone else can keep an eye out too.

She also notices that Josh seems more relaxed in her lessons over the following weeks, which she takes as enough.

She also makes sure the dance club teacher knows that Josh might come, so that he is welcomed by name rather than noticed as new.

steps.label: Model the language
steps.text:
Over the term, she makes a point of using neutral words when talking about families and relationships, such as parents rather than mum and dad and partner rather than girlfriend, and of treating same-sex couples in examples exactly as she treats any couple. None of this is a lesson about orientation. It is the background against which the boys decide whether school is a safe place.

She also notices how often she had, without thinking, used girls and boys as examples of couples in worked problems, and changes her examples.

She also asks the school library to make sure that its fiction shelves include books with gay characters, without fuss.

She also notices that she had sometimes laughed when a colleague called something "a bit gay" in the staff room, and stops.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
The slur does not stop entirely, but it becomes rarer, and twice Martina hears a boy say "Not that word" to another before she can. Josh joins the dance club. In the summer term, a different boy in the class comes out to a friend, and the friend tells Martina later that he had chosen to because, he said, the PE teacher had made it feel all right. Martina had never guessed about either boy, which she thinks is probably why it worked.

Her colleague, the following term, interrupts a similar comment himself. She takes it as the best sign that the change has spread.

She also mentions the approach at a staff meeting, and two other teachers adopt it.

moreFailures.title: Overdoing acceptance
moreFailures.body:
Some people, wanting to show that they are on side, overcorrect. They gush when a colleague mentions a husband, tell him how much they love gay people, introduce him to others as "my gay friend", ask intimate questions about how he knew or how the relationship works, or bring up the subject whenever he is around. It is usually well meant, and it can feel as exposing as hostility. It marks the person as different, makes their orientation the main thing about them, and puts them in the position of managing your enthusiasm. The safe response this chapter describes is ordinary: ask about his weekend in the same tone you would use with anyone, ask what his husband does for a living, and then talk about something else. Being treated as unremarkable is, for most people, the point. If you want to show support, do it through what you do when it matters, such as interrupting a joke.

A simple test is whether you would say the same thing, in the same tone, if he had mentioned a wife.

And remember that coming out to you is not an invitation to make it a topic every time you see him.

moreFailures.title: Assuming straight by default
moreFailures.body:
Most people, without thinking, assume that the person in front of them is straight unless they have been told otherwise. "Have you got a girlfriend?", "What does your wife do?", "Bring your husband" all carry the assumption, and each one puts a gay or bisexual person in the position of either correcting you, which means coming out on your timetable, or letting the assumption stand, which means hiding. Neither choice is theirs. The Neutral by Default drill in this chapter addresses this directly: use "partner" or "anyone special" until you are told otherwise, and mirror the words people use about their own relationships. It costs nothing, it is natural once it becomes a habit, and it quietly tells everyone you speak to that you have not decided who they are before they have told you.

It also helps on forms and invitations, where "partner" or "guest" includes everyone without anyone having to explain.

When someone corrects your assumption, say thank you and use their words; an apology that goes on too long makes the correction harder for them.

Over time, it becomes so ordinary that you stop noticing you are doing it, which is when it helps most.

moreFailures.title: Reading orientation from a partner
moreFailures.body:
When people see a man with a woman, they usually assume he is straight; when they see him with a man, they assume he is gay. For bisexual men, and for anyone whose orientation is not fixed by their current relationship, both readings can be wrong. Bisexual people often describe being treated as confused, as "really" gay or "really" straight depending on who they are dating, or as their partner's orientation rather than their own. A man who has told you he is bisexual remains bisexual whether his partner is a man or a woman, as Ollie did. The broader principle is the one this chapter keeps returning to: orientation is what a person tells you it is, not what you infer from who they are with, how they walk or what they like. When someone tells you, believe them, and do not reinterpret it from the evidence of your own eyes.

The same applies to anyone who tells you how they identify. Their account of themselves is the only reliable one.

It is also worth noticing that bisexual people are often less likely to come out at all, partly because of this kind of rereading.

moreFailures.title: Outing someone by accident
moreFailures.body:
When a colleague or friend has told you about their partner, it can be easy to forget that they may not have told everyone. Mentioning a man's husband to a client, a new colleague or a relative who has not been told takes a decision that belongs to him and makes it for him, in front of people he may have had good reasons to keep it from. It happens most often in passing, in a perfectly friendly sentence: "How's Mark? Are you two still going to Spain?" In some families, workplaces and countries, the consequences can be serious. If someone has told you about a same-sex partner, do not assume that everyone else knows. In new company, follow their lead and let them mention it first. If you are not sure, ask privately: "Is it fine to mention Mark at the client dinner, or would you rather I didn't?"

A good habit is to ask once, early, who knows, and then follow that answer every time.

The same care applies online: tagging someone in a photo with their partner can tell people they have not told.

questions.q: Is it ever all right to ask someone whether they are gay?
questions.a:
Very rarely, and almost never as a way of satisfying curiosity. The question puts the person on the spot and takes away their choice about when and how to tell you, as Ian discovered at the dinner table. If you are close to someone and you sense that they want to talk, you can usually create an opening without asking the question directly: show warmth towards queer people in what you say and do, use neutral language and make it clear that you would not change how you treat anyone. If someone wants you to know, they will tell you. If there is a genuine practical reason to know, such as arranging accommodation for a partner at a work event, ask about the practical thing instead: "Would you like to bring anyone?"

If you are a manager, the same applies to every invitation: let people tell you who they would like to bring.

And if you have already asked, and they said no, believe them, and do not ask again.

A simple rule: be the kind of person someone would want to tell, and leave the timing to them.

questions.q: How can I show that I am a safe person to come out to?
questions.a:
Mostly through what you do when nobody is coming out. React to same-sex couples, on the street or on screen, exactly as you would to anyone. Use neutral words such as partner until you are told otherwise. Do not speculate about anyone's orientation, and do not laugh along when others do. Interrupt jokes and slurs quietly, as Matt did with a plain "Leave it", and as Martina did in the changing room. When someone mentions a same-sex partner, respond with ordinary interest, without surprise or gushing. People who are deciding whether to tell you are usually watching for exactly these things, often for a long time, and they will have learned a great deal about you before you know they were watching.

Small signals matter. A rainbow lanyard means little on its own; how you react to the next joke means a great deal.

If someone does come out to you, keep it to yourself unless they tell you otherwise. Their trust is the reward for everything above.

questions.q: What should I do if a man shows interest in me and I am not interested?
questions.a:
Say no clearly and kindly, as you would to anyone. A man who asks you out, flirts or holds your gaze has done nothing wrong, and the chapter on attraction in Part III applies here unchanged: interest is not an insult, and the only reliable answer to it is a clear one. Something like Jordan's reply works well: "That's kind of you, but I'm straight. I'm happy to stay friends." Avoid recoiling, laughing, telling others about it or treating the man differently afterwards, all of which can be humiliating and, for a gay man in a hostile setting, frightening. If someone continues after a clear no, that is a different matter, and the same advice applies as with any unwanted attention: say it again plainly, move away and get help if you need it.

It also helps to remember that asking took some courage. A kind no respects that.

If you are a gay man and the interest is from a straight woman, the same kind, clear answer applies.

And if the man is a colleague, keep working with him exactly as before. A kind no should not change anything else.

questions.q: I think my teenager might be gay. Should I ask?
questions.a:
It is usually better not to. A direct question, however warm, can feel like being watched and put on the spot, and many young people say they want to tell their parents in their own time, in their own words. Instead, make it obvious that it would be safe to tell you, without saying so in a way that points at them. React warmly to queer people in the news and on television, use neutral language about relationships, challenge jokes and slurs in the family, and keep the general message clear: that you love them whoever they are. Respect their privacy and their friendships. If they do tell you, the most important thing is the first few seconds: thank them, keep your face and voice warm and steady, and do not ask a string of questions straight away.

If they never tell you, that is their choice too, and the love you show them still counts.

If you need support yourself, there are organisations for parents of queer young people that can help you think it through.

And keep loving them out loud in ordinary ways. That is the message they most need to hear, whatever they eventually tell you.

questions.q: Isn't gaydar just a kind of pattern recognition?
questions.a:
It feels like one, but the research suggests that most of what it recognises is stereotypes. Johnson and colleagues found that observers relied heavily on gender stereotypes, such as a sway of the hips, when judging orientation from how people walked. Cox and colleagues found that apparent accuracy from faces could be explained by differences in the photographs, and that telling people gaydar was real made them more willing to stereotype. And because only a small share of people are gay, even a modest accuracy in the laboratory turns into mostly wrong guesses in real life, the false positive paradox described in this chapter. A habit that is wrong most of the time, and that can out or harm people when it is right, is not a skill worth having.

It is also worth noticing how often the stereotypes behind gaydar are the same ones used to bully boys who do not fit.

It also helps to notice when you feel certain about someone. Certainty is usually the stereotype talking.

And the cost of a wrong guess falls on the person guessed about, never on the person guessing.

questions.q: What if I have already made a guess or a joke I regret?
questions.a:
Stop doing it, and do not make the person comfort you about it. If the joke or guess was about someone who heard it, a short, private apology can help: "I'm sorry about what I said. It wasn't OK, and I won't do it again." Do not use the apology as an opportunity to ask about their orientation, and do not make a long speech about how bad you feel, which puts them in the position of reassuring you. If the joke was among friends or colleagues, the most useful thing you can do now is to interrupt the next one, as Gareth eventually did. Most people have joined in with something like this at some point. What matters is what you do the next time it starts.

If you are a parent, the same applies to jokes at home: children remember who laughed.

It also helps to notice whether the people around you still laugh at the same jokes after you have stopped.

watch.title: Heartstopper: Official Trailer
watch.notice: Two schoolboys working out whether a friendship is something more. Notice the held glances, the hesitant touches and the moments they check who is watching: a dialect of interest made careful by uncertainty and risk.

watch.title: Moonlight: Official Trailer
watch.notice: A young Black man growing up gay in Miami. Notice how much is said without words, and how tightly masculinity constrains what the body is allowed to show, even between men who care for each other.

reviewPrompt: This week, put down one guess about someone's orientation, and use partner until you are told otherwise.
